newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asian democrats urge arms, aid embargo on Burma.
newsitem.headline: Asian democrats urge arms, aid embargo on Burma.

text.p: Leading Asian democrats on Monday called for an arms and economic embargo against Burma and urged the international business community to freeze investments until a new government is in place in Rangoon.

The democrats, led by former Philippine president Corazon Aquino and South Korean opposition leader Kim Dae-Jung, also urged the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to withhold any decision admitting Burma as a member.
They said ASEAN's policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma's military rulers, who stand accused of widespread human rights abuses, had been a failure.

In a strongly worded "Manila declaration", the democrats condemned "the recent tightening of controls over the Burmese people" and declared "unstinting support" for Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her supporters.

"The SLORC continues to reject dialogue and has recently employed methods of arrest, detention and public propaganda against the democratic forces in Burma," the declaration said, referring to the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council.

Delegates from about 20 countries approved the declaration at the end of a two-day meeting in Manila organised by the Forum of Democratic Leaders in the Asia-Pacific, a non-government group co-chaired by Aquino and Kim.
Conference delegates "urge China and ASEAN to join an arms embargo on Burma as observed by the United States and the European Union", the declaration said.
Burmese delegates said SLORC had bought more than $1.8 billion worth of arms from China since seizing power in 1988.
The democrats "urge the international business community not to invest in Burma until a government regarded (as) legitimate by the Burmese people is in place", the declaration said.
They also called on international aid and lending agencies "not to resume multilateral or bilateral assistance" to Burma.
In an obvious reference to Burma's application for membership in the ASEAN, they urged "that no steps be taken or allowed which may be construed as encouraging legitimacy of the SLORC regime".
Burma is an observer in the ASEAN and hopes to become a full member at its next formal meeting in July. ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

ASEAN has previously pursued what it describes as a policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma, hoping to bring about change through persuasion, but several members have recently indicated they are having second thoughts about admitting it as a member.
The resolution also called on Japan, as the world's largest economic assistance donor, to take a leading role in convincing the SLORC to enter into "decisive political and economic reform".
The conference also asked SLORC to allow Kim and Aquino to visit Burma and meet with government leaders, Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi and ethnic minorities.
Kim told Reuters the declaration was part of an international campaign Asian democrats had launched to persuade SLORC to relax its grip.
"We must expedite our efforts to keep pressure over the Burmese government," he said.
